::: {#sol-unit-fractions}

1. For $n = 1$, the left side is $\frac{1}{2}$ and the right side is $\frac{1}{2}$.
   For $n = 2$, the left side is $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{2}{3}$ and the right side is $\frac{2}{3}$.
   For $n = 3$, the left side is $\frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{12} = \frac{3}{4}$ and the right side is $\frac{3}{4}$.

2. Suppose $\frac{1}{1 \cdot 2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{k(k + 1)} = \frac{k}{k + 1}$.
   Then

   $$
   \ba
   & \frac{1}{1 \cdot 2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{k(k + 1)} + \frac{1}{(k + 1)(k + 2)}
   \\&= \frac{k}{k + 1} + \frac{1}{(k + 1)(k + 2)}
   && \text{(the supposition)}
   \\&= \frac{k(k + 2) + 1}{(k + 1)(k + 2)}
   && \text{(common denominator)}
   \\&= \frac{k^2 + 2k + 1}{(k + 1)(k + 2)}
   \\&= \frac{(k + 1)^2}{(k + 1)(k + 2)}
   && \text{(} k^2 + 2k + 1 = (k + 1)^2 \text{)}
   \\&= \frac{k + 1}{k + 2},
   && \text{(cancel } k + 1 \text{)}
   \ea
   $$

   which is the claim for $k + 1$.

Part 1 shows the claim for $n = 1$,
and part 2 carries it from each natural number to the next,
so it holds for $n = 2, 3, 4, \ldots$ in turn.

:::
